name: Tip plasty with tongue-in-groove

lead: Tongue-in-groove is a nasal tip technique used in open rhinoplasty. The two medial crura, the paired cartilages in the tip and columella, are sutured to the septum or a septal extension graft, which steadies them and lets the surgeon set the tip's rotation and projection.

The appearance goal is a more defined and better-positioned nasal tip, for example raising a drooping tip or setting a projected, refined tip. A range of studies, including comparisons with columellar strut grafts and randomized trials against other tip techniques, have examined its effect on tip rotation, projection and elasticity.

paras: It is done by a surgeon as part of a rhinoplasty, usually through an open approach with a columellar incision, which gives better visualization and tip precision. The cartilages are positioned and fixed with sutures. Healing involves swelling that, per Wikipedia, can take at least a year to resolve fully.

These are the general risks of rhinoplasty: swelling and bruising, contour irregularities, and a need for revision surgery in roughly 5 to 20% of cases per Wikipedia. Studies compare tongue-in-groove to other tip techniques for how much tip rotation and projection change over time. Surgeon choice and experience matter; smoking impairs healing.

angle.text: The technique gives the surgeon control over where the tip sits and how it is supported, so the tip can be rotated, projected or set back as the plan requires.

lead: Tip plasty with tongue-in-groove is a method of controlling the nasal tip during rhinoplasty. The medial crura of the lower lateral cartilages are fixed to the septum or a septal extension, so the tip's rotation, projection and support are set by how the crura are positioned along that fixed structure. This is part of the wider field of nasal tip refinement and support, which Wikipedia describes as using columellar struts or septal extension grafts [1].

Surgeons describe it in titles such as 'Effects of the Tongue-in-Groove Maneuver on Nasal Tip Rotation' (Aesthetic Surgery Journal, 2018) and 'Tongue-in-Groove Setback of the Medial Crura to Control Nasal Tip Deprojection in Open Rhinoplasty' (Aesthetic Plastic Surgery, 2015) [2]. Studies compare it with other tip techniques: a 2020 paper on elastic properties of the nasal tip one year after columellar strut graft versus tongue-in-groove, a 2021 comparison of tongue-in-groove and septocolumellar suture with a short, floating strut on tip rotation and projection, and a 2022 randomized controlled trial of cartilage remodeling using lateral crural steal and tongue-in-groove [2].

paras: In rhinoplasty, tip support is typically provided by a columellar strut or a septal extension graft; Wikipedia says the septal extension graft gives greater control and changes less over time [1]. Tongue-in-groove is one of several suture-based ways of fixing the medial crura to a stable structure so the tip holds its position.

The open approach adds a columellar incision and gives better visualization and tip precision; it is usually preferred in revision surgery. Closed rhinoplasty keeps all incisions inside the nose with less swelling and faster recovery, and systematic reviews find no significant long-term difference in outcomes, according to Wikipedia [1].

Wikipedia says revision rhinoplasty is needed in roughly 5 to 20% of cases, that smoking impairs healing, and that swelling can take at least a year to resolve [1]. Tip-support choices affect how much the tip rotates or projects over time, which is the focus of comparative studies [2].

Published studies on tongue-in-groove include a 2018 Aesthetic Surgery Journal paper on effects on nasal tip rotation, a 2015 paper on setback of the medial crura to control tip deprojection, a 2020 comparison of tip elasticity one year after columellar strut graft versus tongue-in-groove, a 2021 comparison with septocolumellar suture and a floating strut, a 2022 randomized controlled trial of cartilage remodeling in nasal tip rhinoplasty using lateral crural steal and tongue-in-groove, and a 2024 comparison of one-year tip projection with a flexible tongue-in-groove triple cartilage suture versus the classical technique [2]. The result listings do not include the findings.
